description: Time-breakdown diagnosis (draft forward / target forward / cache-crop / unaccounted Python overhead) for cached vs non-cached speculative decoding, run at two generation lengths to test whether the short-length slowdown is compute-bound or overhead-bound.
interpretation: At 60 tokens, cached is slower overall (0.698x): crop time is negligible (~4ms, ruled out as a cause) and unaccounted (Python/cache bookkeeping) overhead is higher for cached (+0.263s) but is not the dominant term -- the dominant term is that cached's own draft+target model-forward time is HIGHER than no-cache's, despite processing fewer tokens per call, consistent with per-call MPS dispatch overhead dominating over the (still small at this length) savings from not reprocessing history. At 400 tokens, this reverses: cached's draft+target time is now substantially LOWER than no-cache's (no-cache's cost of reprocessing a growing history has become large enough to matter), more than offsetting cached's larger (both absolutely and, at this length, proportionally) bookkeeping overhead, giving a net 1.249x speedup. This profiling-instrumented 1.249x differs from the non-instrumented p5_kv_cache_speedup_400_result.json's 1.651x at the same 400-token length because the profiling script's extra torch.mps.synchronize() calls (needed for accurate per-bucket timing) add overhead disproportionately to the cached path (which makes many more, smaller model calls per round) -- the non-instrumented number is the one to cite as representative.
